metadata.title: The role of computer game playing and reading attitudes in digital reading achievement: evidence from Hong Kong 15-year-olds
metadata.venue: Research and Practice in Technology Enhanced Learning

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study used the Hong Kong subset of PISA 2018 and incorporated PISA’s two-stage stratified sampling design by applying the final student weight (W_FSTUWT) together with 80 replicate weights (W_FSTURWT 1–80). Weights were implemented in R using the svrepdesign function from the survey package, and the authors explicitly state this was done to obtain unbiased parameter estimates and correct standard errors. The analysis also used the full set of ten plausible values for the digital reading achievement components (RCLI, RCUN, RCER), consistent with OECD recommendations for PV-based achievement estimation. Beyond weighting and PV use, preprocessing included reverse-coding negatively phrased reading-attitude items and scaling/centering variables prior to structural equation modeling.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used the Hong Kong sample from PISA 2018 (15-year-olds in secondary schools) and analyzed student-level questionnaire and ICT familiarity questionnaire variables. Digital reading achievement was represented by the three reading components (RCLI, RCUN, RCER) using all ten plausible values for each component. The analytic sample corresponds to N = 6037 Hong Kong students; missingness was handled via FIML within the structural equation modeling framework rather than listwise/pairwise deletion.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Structural equation modeling (Model 2/3): computer game playing → digital reading achievement (direct βc = -0.04, SE = 0.02, p = .02 in Model 2; βc = 0.01, SE = 0.02, p = .60 in Model 3). Indirect effect via reading attitudes: βa*b = -0.06 (SE = 0.01, p = .02) in Model 2; βa*b = -0.03 (p < .001) in Model 3. Total effect in Model 2: βc+a*b = -0.10 (SE = 0.02, p < .001). Model fit (Model 3): CFI = .97, RMSEA = .08, SRMR = .07.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Hong Kong 15-year-olds digital reading data (RCLI/RCUN/RCER plausible values), the study leveraged computer game playing and reading attitudes (with gender controlled) to analyze digital reading achievement, finding that computer game playing had a negative association with digital reading achievement that became non-significant after accounting for reading attitudes (direct effect βc = 0.01, p = .60) while the indirect (mediated) pathway remained significant (βa*b = -0.03, p < .001). This indicates that strengthening reading attitudes may be a key lever to buffer the negative impact of excessive gaming on digitally assessed reading performance, though the cross-sectional mediation cannot establish causal effects.

data.outcome_summary: This study analyzed the Hong Kong subset of PISA 2018 (N = 6,037 15-year-olds) to examine how computer game playing and reading attitudes relate to digital reading achievement, and whether reading attitudes mediate the gaming–achievement relationship under gender control. Digital reading achievement was modeled using the three PISA digital reading components (RCLI, RCUN, RCER) represented by all ten plausible values, while computer game playing and reading attitudes were latent factors measured from ICT familiarity and student questionnaire items. Using confirmatory factor analysis and structural equation modeling (lavaan/lavaan.survey) with PISA’s final weight (W_FSTUWT) and 80 replicate weights, the authors found that computer game playing was negatively associated with both reading attitudes and digital reading achievement, and that reading attitudes positively predicted digital reading achievement. In Model 2, both direct and indirect effects were significant; in Model 3, the direct effect of gaming on achievement became non-significant while the indirect effect through reading attitudes remained significant (βa*b = -0.03, p < .001). Limitations include reliance on cross-sectional PISA data and SEM mediation assumptions rather than causal identification.
data.null_fields_interpretation: The paper uses confirmatory factor analysis and structural equation modeling (SEM) to test correlations and mediation among latent variables, not machine-learning prediction/classification. As a result, no ML algorithms (per the schema’s ML-only list) are evaluated, so ml_techniques.all_techniques is empty and primary is left null. The study’s substantive results are therefore extracted as SEM mediation effects rather than predictive ML performance.
